q: Why can a rising serum creatinine be pathological even when it remains near the laboratory normal range?
o: A value at the upper limit of normal excludes significant loss of renal function
Serum creatinine should rise with normal aging and need not affect renal drug dosing
Creatinine production increases as muscle mass falls, so a rising level is normal aging
Since there is also a steady loss of muscle mass with age, with a concomitant reduction in creatinine production, serum creatinine should remain relatively constant.
explanation:
Since there is also a steady loss of muscle mass with age, with a concomitant reduction in creatinine production, serum creatinine should remain relatively constant. (p1268).

C. Creatinine production increases as muscle mass falls, so a rising level is normal aging: The book describes reduced creatinine production with loss of muscle mass (p1268).
A. A value at the upper limit of normal excludes significant loss of renal function: The book states that an upper-normal level can represent significant decline in an older individual (p1268).
B. Serum creatinine should rise with normal aging and need not affect renal drug dosing: The book says creatinine should remain relatively constant and elevations warrant attention to renal function and dosing (p1268).

q: Is proteinuria an expected consequence of normal human aging?
o: Proteinuria is always a pathological finding and requires a full work-up.
Proteinuria can be dismissed as normal aging if creatinine remains within its normal range
Proteinuria is expected whenever normal aging reduces GFR and needs no work-up
Proteinuria is a normal feature of human kidney aging, as it is in rats
explanation:
Proteinuria is always a pathological finding and requires a full work-up. (p1269).

D. Proteinuria is a normal feature of human kidney aging, as it is in rats: The book explicitly distinguishes humans from rodent models (p1269).
C. Proteinuria is expected whenever normal aging reduces GFR and needs no work-up: Despite declining GFR, proteinuria is not a normal feature of aging (p1269).
B. Proteinuria can be dismissed as normal aging if creatinine remains within its normal range: The book requires a work-up of proteinuria; an upper-normal creatinine can itself reflect significant loss of function (p1269; p1268).

q: As GFR declines, how does potassium fractional excretion differ in older versus younger adults?
o: the fractional excretion of potassium does not rise as much as in young individuals
It rises more than in young individuals because aldosterone levels increase
A smaller fractional-excretion rise means unstressed serum potassium cannot remain normal
It rises equally in all age groups, without an aldosterone-related difference
explanation:
As GFR declines, fractional potassium excretion does not rise as much in older adults, partly because of lower aldosterone levels or resistance. Unstressed serum potassium may remain normal (p1270).

B. It rises more than in young individuals because aldosterone levels increase: The rise is smaller, partly due to lower aldosterone or aldosterone resistance (p1270).
D. It rises equally in all age groups, without an aldosterone-related difference: The book describes a smaller rise in older adults and an aldosterone-related mechanism (p1270).
C. A smaller fractional-excretion rise means unstressed serum potassium cannot remain normal: Normal serum potassium under unstressed conditions is explicitly described despite the age-related limitation (p1270).

q: Does absence of typical ECG changes exclude dangerous hyperkalemia?
o: the absence of ECG findings in the presence of a high potassium level should not lead the clinician to conclude that the hyperkalemia is erroneous or insignificant
The same potassium concentration always produces the same ECG findings
Dangerous hyperkalemia always produces the classic ordered ECG progression
Absence of ECG changes proves that an elevated potassium result is erroneous
explanation:
the absence of ECG findings in the presence of a high potassium level should not lead the clinician to conclude that the hyperkalemia is erroneous or insignificant (p1271).

D. Absence of ECG changes proves that an elevated potassium result is erroneous: The book specifically rejects this conclusion (p1271).
C. Dangerous hyperkalemia always produces the classic ordered ECG progression: That progression is seldom seen; manifestations may be subtle (p1271).
B. The same potassium concentration always produces the same ECG findings: The same level may produce vastly different ECG effects (p1271).

q: What makes podocyte loss important in the proposed sclerosis mechanism?
o: These specialized cells are postmitotic and if damaged in any way, cannot be replaced.
The proposed mechanism preserves every nephron despite complete glomerular sclerosis
Podocyte detachment leaves the filtration barrier fully covered and prevents sclerosis
Podocytes multiply in proportion to glomerular tuft enlargement
explanation:
Podocytes are postmitotic and cannot be replaced. Their detachment with tuft expansion is believed to expose basement membrane and initiate sclerosis (p1272).

D. Podocytes multiply in proportion to glomerular tuft enlargement: Unlike endothelial and mesangial cells, podocytes cannot multiply to match increasing tuft volume (p1272).
C. Podocyte detachment leaves the filtration barrier fully covered and prevents sclerosis: Detachment exposes basement membrane and is thought to trigger sclerosis (p1272).
B. The proposed mechanism preserves every nephron despite complete glomerular sclerosis: An entire glomerulus can sclerose and shrivel with loss of that nephron and filtration capacity (p1272).

q: Does the chapter establish protein restriction as prevention of normal human kidney aging?
o: Protein restriction was much more effective than caloric restriction in the rat studies
The human vegetarian comparison showed preserved kidney function only in the lower-protein group
Animal studies establish protein restriction as prevention of normal human kidney aging

There is evidence to support protein restriction in patients with established renal disease to reduce symptoms of uremia, but none to support the role of protein restriction to prevent age-related changes in the human kidney.
explanation:
There is evidence to support protein restriction in patients with established renal disease to reduce symptoms of uremia, but none to support the role of protein restriction to prevent age-related changes in the human kidney. (p1274).

C. Animal studies establish protein restriction as prevention of normal human kidney aging: The relevance of the animal studies in humans remains unclear (p1274).
A. Protein restriction was much more effective than caloric restriction in the rat studies: The book reports the opposite: protein restriction was much less effective (p1274).
B. The human vegetarian comparison showed preserved kidney function only in the lower-protein group: The observational comparison showed no differences in kidney function between the groups (p1274).
